questions.question: A user sends a second message in your chat app, but the model does not know what was said in the first message. What is the most likely cause?
options: The API key was different for the second request.
The app sent only the new message instead of the full conversation history.
The system prompt was too short.
The model's context window was full after one message.
questions.explanation: The API is stateless, so the app must send the whole messages list every time. The most tempting wrong option is the API key: the key identifies your account for billing and does not create any memory between requests.

questions.question: A response has stop_reason set to "max_tokens". What does this tell you?
options: The model finished its answer normally.
The model wants to call a tool.
The reply was cut off because it reached the length limit in the request.
The request used more tokens than the model's context window allows.
questions.explanation: max_tokens means the output hit the limit you set, so the reply may be incomplete. The most tempting wrong option is the context window: that limit covers the whole request, and a request that is too long is rejected with an error instead of returning a cut-off reply.

questions.question: You are starting development on a paid LLM API. Which setup keeps both risk and cost lowest?
options: Store the key in an environment variable, set a monthly spend limit, use a smaller model and a low max_tokens.
Put the key in the code so it cannot be lost, and use the largest model to get the best results.
Store the key in a .env file that is committed to Git, so teammates can use it.
Use a high max_tokens so that replies are never cut off, and check the bill at the end of the month.
questions.explanation: An environment variable keeps the key out of code, and the spend limit, smaller model and low max_tokens keep costs small while testing. The most tempting wrong option is a committed .env file: once a key is in Git history, anyone with access to the repository can use it, so it must be replaced.

questions.question: Your support app puts customer messages inside <customer_message> tags and the system prompt says the tags contain data. What is the main benefit?
options: It makes the model reply faster.
It reduces the price per token.
It removes the need for a system prompt.
It helps the model tell your instructions apart from the user's text.
questions.explanation: Tags separate instructions from data, which improves reliability and makes injected instructions less effective. The most tempting wrong option is removing the need for a system prompt: the tags only work because the system prompt explains what they contain.

questions.question: A chat app sends a 2,000-token system prompt and the full history with every request. Users complain about cost and speed. Which change best addresses both?
options: Raise max_tokens so that answers are more complete.
Send only the parts of the history and context the model needs, and keep max_tokens realistic.
Switch the conversation to a language that looks shorter on screen.
Remove the usage logging to save time.
questions.explanation: Fewer input tokens and a realistic output limit reduce both cost and latency. The most tempting wrong option is changing language: text that looks shorter does not always use fewer tokens, and the change would harm users; you must measure tokens with the token counter.
